name: Bulletproof diet

lead: The Bulletproof diet was created by entrepreneur Dave Asprey, who published a buttered-coffee recipe in 2009 and the book The Bulletproof Diet in 2014. It centres on a blended drink of coffee, MCT oil and grass-fed butter or ghee, with a high-fat, moderate-protein, low-carbohydrate plan and intermittent fasting.

Followers say the coffee gives energy and fullness through the morning, which they use to eat less and stay lean for a better physique. Small studies have measured effects of the drink on cognition, satiety and inflammation markers, while dietitians have questioned many of the broader claims.

paras: People typically replace a morning meal with the blended coffee and continue with fatty foods such as grass-fed beef and butter, avoiding items the plan labels harmful. It is often combined with intermittent fasting and weight training; T Nation members mention drinking it before workouts or during a fasting window.

Critics note that the drink adds a large amount of saturated fat and calories, and the British Dietetic Association lists the diet as a fad diet. The FDA sent a warning letter in 2021 about product claims. People with lipid or digestive conditions are usually advised to ask a clinician.

angle.text: Users say the drink helps them fast or eat low-carb, which they use to stay lean. The effect on appearance depends on overall energy balance and training.

lead: The Bulletproof diet is a high-fat, moderate-protein, low-carbohydrate eating plan created by American entrepreneur Dave Asprey. Its signature item, Bulletproof Coffee, is coffee blended with medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil and grass-fed butter or ghee. Asprey says he developed it after drinking yak-butter tea in Tibet and posted a recipe in 2009.[1]

Within looksmaxxing and fitness communities it is used as a way to stay full during fasting windows, to keep carbohydrate intake low and to support training, which in turn is aimed at a leaner, more muscular look.[2][3] A T Nation poster described using the coffee first thing before a home workout, and another said it kept him going at work.[2][4]

A small amount of published research has examined the drink. Studies in young healthy adults have looked at its effects on cognitive function and satiety, and on markers of cellular inflammation.[5][6]
infobox: Coffee, MCT oil, grass-fed butter or ghee

paras: The plan emphasises grass-fed beef and butter, intermittent fasting and the buttered coffee. It labels foods such as soy, wheat, canned vegetables and microwaved foods as harmful. Asprey also warns about mycotoxins in coffee and sells a coffee he markets as free of them.[1]

Asprey worked in technology at firms including Trend Micro, Blue Coat Systems and Citrix. He founded Bulletproof 360 in 2013 and Bulletproof Nutrition in 2014, published the book in 2014 and raised $9 million from Trinity Ventures in July 2015. He stepped down as CEO in September 2019.[1] A 2014 Hacker News thread discussed the diet as a cult-like phenomenon.[7]

Asprey has said the coffee together with other practices raised his IQ by more than 20 points, and attributes inflammation to mycotoxins.[1] Fitness-forum users mention it as a way to get through fasting periods.[3]

The British Dietetic Association lists the diet among fad diets, and dietitians quoted in coverage say any alertness is from caffeine. Journalist Julia Belluz wrote that Asprey ignored contrary studies. Stephan Guyenet said some advice, such as eating whole foods, is healthful.[1]

A regulatory history exists: the FTC sent Asprey a warning letter in 2020 about COVID-19 claims for vitamin products, and the FDA wrote to Bulletproof 360 in 2021 stating its products were not generally recognized as safe and effective for their advertised uses.[1]

A single-blind, randomized crossover study compared Bulletproof Coffee (coffee, MCT oil and grass-fed ghee) with black coffee for effects on cognitive function and satiety.[5] A separate study in young healthy humans examined coffee containing MCT oil and ghee on markers of cellular inflammation, motivated by the concern that acute high-fat intake can promote endotoxemia.[6]

lore.intro: On strength and fitness forums, the coffee is a common fasting-window tool.

claims.claim: Butter coffee keeps you full through a fast.
